title: Cross-Domain Sycophancy: Does Domain Expertise of Framing Change Capitulation Rate?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Knowing domain-specific sycophancy vulnerability guides deployment warnings and targeted interventions. Useful but incremental: it refines understanding of an existing problem rather than identifying a new one.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Constructing matched false-premise questions across domains and testing via API is very accessible. No model training needed. Prompt engineering across 6 domains with authority framing variations is well within beginner capability.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear deliverable: capitulation rate table across domains and framing conditions. Well-defined 2-factor experimental design. 6 domains x 2 framing conditions is manageable. 30 hours is ample.

novelty.reasoning: The key question — whether domain expertise framing modulates sycophancy — has been directly answered. (1) 'When Truth Is Overridden' (arXiv:2508.02087, 2025) uses logit-lens and causal activation patching to show sycophancy is opinion-driven, NOT authority-driven. User expertise framing (e.g., 'as a professor') has negligible impact, while first-person grammatical framing ('I believe') has a 13.6% increase. (2) SycEval-EM (arXiv:2601.16529, 2026) tests across clinical domains with five persuasion tactics, finding uniform 30-36% acquiescence regardless of tactic type. (3) ELEPHANT measures domain-varying social sycophancy. The core finding this idea would produce — that expertise framing does not significantly change capitulation rates — is already established in the literature.
